query: What missing-data workflow (FIML vs MI, number of imputations, auxiliary variables) and MNAR sensitivity analyses should we preregister for primary and mediation models?

response.query: What missing-data workflow (FIML vs MI, number of imputations, auxiliary variables) and MNAR sensitivity analyses should we preregister for primary and mediation models?
response.answer: For primary and mediation models, use full information maximum likelihood (FIML) or multiple imputation (MI) with at least 10 imputations and include auxiliary variables. Conduct MNAR sensitivity analyses.

results.title: [PDF] Missing Data and Missing Data Estimation in SEM
results.content: Newsom Psy 523/623 Structural Equation Modeling, Spring 2025 2 FIML Probably the most pragmatic missing data estimation approach for structural equation modeling is full information maximum likelihood (FIML), which has been shown to produce unbiased parameter estimates and standard errors under MAR and MCAR (Enders & Bandalos, 2001). Multiple imputation (MI; see Graham & Hofer, 2000; Schafer, 1997) is another modern missing data approach that produces unbiased estimates and efficient standard errors, and is comparable to FIML, assuming MAR and MCAR assumption. Even if the mechanism is not MCAR or MAR (i.e., data are MNAR), modern missing data estimation (FIML or MI) will be preferable to listwise deletion if appropriate auxiliary variables are included in the model, because their inclusion reduces the impact of MNAR (Graham, 2009; although see Thoemmes & Rose, 2014, for some exceptions).

results.title: How and why to follow best practices for testing mediation models with missing data
results.content: However, FIML or MI are rarely used to handle missing data when testing mediation models, instead analyses used listwise deletion methods, the default in popular software. Listwise deletion is the default method for most software packages and can provide estimates and tests of the indirect effect; however, estimates are only unbiased when missing data are MCAR. FIML is limited in the software it is implemented in, however, FIML provides powerful and accurate estimates of the indirect effect when data are MCAR or MAR, assuming appropriate auxiliary variables are included in the model. Using _R_ and the associated packages, missing data can be handled using either MI or FIML and indirect effects can be tested with bootstrap confidence intervals (using FIML), the joint significance test or Monte Carlo confidence intervals. In the examples below we fit both cross‐sectional and three time‐point longitudinal mediation models using _R_ and _JASP_ and compare the results across different methods of missing data handling (i.e., listwise deletion, MI and FIML), and different methods of testing the indirect effect (i.e., bootstrapping, the joint significance test and Monte Carlo confidence intervals). As with many software programmes using FIML, participants with missing data on any of the auxiliary variables were listwise deleted, though the participants with missing data on the variables in the analysis model is handled with the FIML estimator using the information from the auxiliary variables to help inform the process. Even though a few participants' data were not included in the FIML model due to missing on the auxiliary variables, the majority of the sample size was maintained (97.13%) which produced a higher quality parameter estimate representative of the population value, as well as maintain the similar power level of the original sample (_N_ = 522) to detect significance of the indirect effect in particular. Compared to the second, which included only the auxiliary variables used in the cross‐sectional model from time 1, the number of parameters estimated was 177 and the missing data patterns handled was 63. However, in a mediation model this only applies to the X variable, as both M and Y are outcomes and listwise deletion still results in power loses compared to other missing data methods.

results.title: missing data methods in randomized controlled nutrition trials
results.content: Some problematic missing data methods such as complete case (CC) analysis and last-observation-carried-forward (LOCF) are unfortunately still common in nutrition trials. In this statistical guidance, we provide a brief introduction of missing data mechanisms and the unreasonable assumptions that underlie CC and LOCF and recommend 2 appropriate missing data methods: multiple imputation and full information maximum likelihood. **Keywords:** missing data, randomized controlled trials, multiple imputation, full information maximum likelihood, missing data mechanisms Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), the gold standard to generate rigorous evidence on intervention effects by providing unbiased causal inference, are common in nutrition research. In this statistical guidance, we briefly introduce the idea of the missing data mechanism, effects of missing data on statistical inference from RCTs, and why CC and single imputation methods including LOCF can lead to incorrect inferences and then recommend 2 appropriate approaches: multiple imputation (MI) and full information maximum likelihood (FIML). MAR is the most common assumption for the modern missing data methods (e.g., MI and FIML). Because this assumption is untestable and unknowable from data, sensitivity analyses are recommended, which specify a range of plausible values for missing data under an MNAR assumption to evaluate the potential departure of statistical estimates and inference from those obtained in the primary analysis under an MAR assumption(1). There are, however, multiple appropriate procedures to handle missing outcome data in RCTs (1), including MI and FIML methods. MI involves imputing values for the missing values (as with single imputation) but doing so multiple times, creating multiple (e.g., 100) “complete” data sets. Unlike MI, missing data are not imputed in this method but handled in the analysis by utilizing a case-wise likelihood function using only the variables that are observed for each case. Both MI and FIML are advanced statistical tools to appropriately handle missing data and can provide unbiased estimates and valid statistical inferences if the MAR assumption holds. Abbreviations used: CC, complete case; FCS, fully conditional specification; FIML, full information maximum likelihood; ITT, intent-to-treat; LOCF, last-observation-carried-forward; MAR, missing at random; MCAR, missing completely at random; MI, multiple imputation; ML, maximum likelihood; MNAR, missing not at random; MVN, multivariate normal; RCT, randomized controlled trial.
